look_here_first: MUCRONATE SPRANGLETOP — think FINE-BRANCHED ANNUAL: an often slender warm-season annual with NUMEROUS almost straight ascending flowering branches scattered along a main axis, like a narrow brush. Check a mature tiny spikelet with 10–20×: typically 2–4 florets in a ca. 2–4 mm laterally flattened spikelet; short glumes and a tiny pointed glume tip (mucro) require a lens, and do NOT by themselves prove subspecies. Look at the leaf sheath for distinct bulbous/papillose-based spreading hairs and examine the true membranous ligule. The existing source photograph shows only broad panicle/leaf features: it cannot certify floret number, sheath-hair bases, glume mucro or mucronata versus other D. panicea subspecies.

best_field_traits: ANNUAL: tufted or several shoots from an annual fibrous-rooted base; not the longer-lived robust perennial green sprangletop.
PANICLE: many rather straight ascending narrow branches along an elongated central axis, often narrow or somewhat brush-like, and with tiny spikelets attached along sides.
SPIKELET: very small, commonly ~2–4 mm long; about 2–4 florets. Under a lens count florets INSIDE one spikelet rather than spikelets along a branch.
GLUMES: narrow bracts subtending each spikelet; the minute MUCRONATE upper tip is a tiny pointed projection, not necessarily a visible long awn. Exact subspecies anatomy remains unphotographed.
LEAF SHEATH: some distinctly spreading hairs can arise from small raised/bulbous or papillose bases; inspect actual sheath with 10–20× rather than assuming in the whole-plant photo.
LIGULE: membranous with fringed/jagged upper margin; measure actual specimen, do not infer from hairs outside the sheath.
TAXONOMY CAUTION: subsp. mucronata is accepted by POWO; historical Leptochloa mucronata is a synonym. Other subspecies in the D. panicea complex may look similar and need voucher-level checks.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Connected WHOLE ANNUAL: rooted fibrous plant, full brush-like panicle and ruler; document lack of perennial rootstock.
PANICLE BRANCH INSERTION: central axis showing many thin, mostly ascending branches with attached spikelets; overall habit alone is provisional.
SPIKELET MACRO 10–20×: mature 2–4 mm spikelet with a millimeter scale, floret count and glumes clearly separated.
UPPER GLUME MACRO 20×: show any actual minute mucro (tiny hard point) and distinguish it from an awn, with photographed glume tip and scale.
LEAF SHEATH AND LIGULE 10–20×: papillose/bulbous hair bases and true membranous leaf-collar ligule; no arrow until photo visibly resolves the structure.
SUBSPECIES CHECK: authenticated herbarium macro for mucronata versus brachiata at same scale; preserve unresolved determination if only a species-level photograph exists.
MATCHED LOOK-ALIKE: side-by-side measured 2–4-flowered Dinebra spikelet and 4–13-flowered Disakisperma spikelet, each with full rooted plant.
crew_field_check: MUCRONATE SPRANGLETOP — think FINE-BRANCHED ANNUAL: an often slender warm-season annual with NUMEROUS almost straight ascending flowering branches scattered along a main axis, like a narrow brush. Check a mature tiny spikelet with 10–20×: typically 2–4 florets in a ca. 2–4 mm laterally flattened spikelet; short glumes and a tiny pointed glume tip (mucro) require a lens, and do NOT by themselves prove subspecies. Look at the leaf sheath for distinct bulbous/papillose-based spreading hairs and examine the true membranous ligule. The existing source photograph shows only broad panicle/leaf features: it cannot certify floret number, sheath-hair bases, glume mucro or mucronata versus other D. panicea subspecies.

GREEN SPRANGLETOP / Disakisperma dubium: generally a larger perennial arising from a lasting base, commonly with fewer longer near-fingerlike branches, and larger 4–12 mm spikelets containing about 4–13 florets. MUCRONATE SPRANGLETOP / Dinebra panicea subsp. mucronata: slender ANNUAL with many ascending slender branches, generally much smaller ~2–4 mm spikelets with ~2–4 florets and often bulbous-based sheath hairs. Counts can overlap at 4 florets, so a single spikelet count isn't decisive. ERAGROSTIS lovegrasses: many have an airy panicle too but individual spikelets have several fertile florets in overlapping ranks, and the branching/spikelet anatomy differs. Within DINEBRA, the other subspecies of D. panicea can look extremely similar; a photograph labeled merely Dinebra panicea is NOT independently sufficient to certify subsp. mucronata. Old Leptochloa mucronata refers to this taxon in the Kew treatment; Leptochloa filiformis and other older names have been applied differently in historical treatments.

If the plant is only photographed as a whole brush-like head, label at most Dinebra panicea complex / sprangletop candidate pending attached glumes and floret measurements. Preserve subspecies record without inventing certainty.

visual_comparison.subtitle: Three real existing source-credited photos: only first is Dinebra, the other two are look-alike comparisons. Existing two gross arrows retained; no verified glume-mucro macro.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: MANY THIN BRANCHES + ANNUAL BASE + TINY USUALLY 2–4-FLORET SPIKELETS suggests Dinebra panicea. Subspecies mucronata needs close botanical determination, not an ordinary photo.

items.label: 2 · GREEN SPRANGLETOP — clearly different species
items.image_role: Existing physically present CC BY-NC green sprangletop comparison only, not an image of Dinebra.
items.caption: This is GREEN SPRANGLETOP (Disakisperma dubium), NOT Dinebra. Compare its generally few, longer one-sided flowering branches and perennial growth with fine-branched annual Dinebra. The 4–13 florets in one spikelet are a botanical key requiring a macro photograph, not a claim verified from this broad photo.
items.why_it_matters: Two commonly called 'sprangletop' grasses need to be separated using a whole plant plus an actual spikelet.
items.creator: John Connolly
items.photo_status: Existing separate taxon photo reused without modification; per-photo NC license/creator retained, microscopic florets not arrowed.

items.caption: This is PLAINS LOVEGRASS (Eragrostis intermedia), NOT Dinebra. Airy panicle branches can deceive from a distance; inspect individual spikelets and count florets rather than relying on a fine-grass silhouette. Spikelet anatomy is not directly resolved in this image.
items.why_it_matters: Prevents overconfident 'sprangletop' naming based only on delicate narrow branches.
